name: Quadriceps (rectus femoris) strain
populations: elite male and female football players
athletes returning after ACL reconstruction with a patellar tendon graft
summary: A tear of the rectus femoris, the two-joint quadriceps muscle, usually from kicking or sprint acceleration, most often near its central tendon or musculotendinous junction in the proximal to mid anterior thigh.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Days to weeks. Mean 20 days to return to full training in elite track and field; central tendon involvement is slower

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free palpation and resisted tests, strength, sprinting and kicking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Localised anterior thigh tenderness with pain on resisted knee extension and hip flexion; a palpable gap suggests a tendon injury

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI at 24–72 h grades the injury and shows central tendon involvement, which predicts a longer rehabilitation

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive kicking and sprinting; the kicking leg is at higher risk

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 19% of muscle injuries in male professional footballers; 11% of all injuries in elite women's football

overview:
Quadriceps strains are common in sports that need repetitive kicking and sprinting, and the rectus femoris is the muscle involved in most cases [r1,r2]. The rectus femoris is the most commonly injured muscle of the anterior thigh among athletes, especially soccer players [r3]. It crosses both the hip and the knee, and it is most often injured at or near its central tendon (the deep aponeurosis in the proximal to mid belly) or at the musculotendinous junction (MTJ) [r2].

Most injuries recover with planned rehabilitation, but the site matters. In a small MRI study of Australian football players, rectus femoris injuries around the central tendon took a mean of 26.9 days to return to full training, against 9.2 days for injuries in the periphery of the muscle [r2]. Complete tendon injuries and avulsions can need surgery [r4]. No randomised trials of treatment for quadriceps strain were identified, so rehabilitation draws on muscle-injury principles and hamstring-injury consensus [r5,r6].

epidemiology.text: In 2908 muscle injuries recorded in male professional footballers, muscle injuries made up 31% of all injuries and the quadriceps accounted for 19% of them, after the hamstrings (37%) and adductors (23%). Sixteen percent of muscle injuries were re-injuries, and these caused longer absences than index injuries [r7]. In the UEFA Elite Club Injury Study, thigh muscle injuries (anterior and posterior combined) made up 25% of all injuries, 88% of them indirect (strain) injuries with a mean absence of 18.5 days, against 7 days for direct injuries [r8]. In elite women's football, thigh muscle injuries were the most common injury, with quadriceps injuries at 11% (171 of 1527) and hamstring injuries at 12% [r9]. A systematic review of risk factors included 16 studies with 2408 quadriceps injuries in 11,719 athletes [r10].

intrinsic: ACL reconstruction with a patellar tendon autograft: in professional male footballers the quadriceps injury rate in the 2 years after return to play was 3.5 times that of the 2 years before the ACL injury (RR 3.5, 95% CI 1.4–8.8) [r11]
Age, body weight and flexibility were not associated with quadriceps injury [r10]
extrinsic: Preseason period and competitive match play [r10]
Fixture congestion: muscle injury rates (specifically hamstring and quadriceps) were higher with 4 or fewer recovery days, RR 1.32 (95% CI 1.15–1.51) for muscle injuries overall [r12]
Participating at a higher level of competition was associated with a lower risk [r10]

mechanism.summary: Quadriceps strains occur in sports that involve repetitive kicking and sprinting [r1]. The rectus femoris is the only biarticular quadriceps muscle: it flexes the hip and extends the knee, so it is lengthened by hip extension combined with knee flexion, as in the back-swing of a kick (mechanism reasoning). In a kick, the lengthened muscle then contracts forcefully to drive hip flexion and knee extension through ball contact. The tear is most often near the central tendon or MTJ in the proximal to mid belly [r2,r4].
sequence: The athlete approaches the ball or accelerates, and the kicking-side rectus femoris is already active.
In the back-swing, the hip extends and the knee flexes, which lengthens the biarticular rectus femoris over both joints (mechanism reasoning).
The muscle then contracts forcefully, driving hip flexion and knee extension towards ball contact, so a lengthened, highly active muscle takes very high load.
Load exceeds the capacity of the weakest region, typically the fibres near the central tendon or the MTJ in the proximal to mid belly [r2].
The athlete feels sudden sharp pain in the front of the thigh and often cannot continue kicking or sprinting.
Bleeding and swelling follow, and pain is provoked by hip flexion and knee extension [r4].
If the tear extends into the central tendon or proximal tendon, recovery is slower and surgical review may be needed [r13,r4].

variants.name: Kicking injury
variants.description: Injury in the kicking leg during back-swing or ball contact. The dominant kicking leg is a risk factor [r10].

variants.name: Sprint or acceleration injury
variants.description: Rectus femoris injuries are common in sports that require maximal acceleration and sprinting. Four complete proximal free tendon injuries in elite track and field athletes happened during sprinting, all in female athletes [r13].

variants.name: Proximal tendon injury
variants.description: Each head of the rectus femoris can be injured at the enthesis, within the tendon or at the MTJ. In children, the typical injury is avulsion of the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) from the direct head, and indirect head injuries may be underdiagnosed [r3].

variants.name: Direct blow (contusion)
variants.description: A direct blow is a different injury. In male elite footballers 12% of thigh muscle injuries were direct, and absence was shorter (7 days) than for indirect injuries [r8].

anatomy.text: The quadriceps has four heads. The vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius each cross only the knee. The rectus femoris crosses both the hip and the knee. It arises from two proximal tendons, the direct head from the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) and the indirect (reflected) head from the superior acetabular rim [r3]. A central tendon (aponeurosis) runs down the proximal to mid belly, and muscle fibres insert onto it. The quadriceps tendon joins the four heads at the patella. The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps.

structures.name: Rectus femoris
structures.role: Biarticular muscle: hip flexor and knee extensor. The most commonly injured anterior thigh muscle in athletes [r3]

structures.name: Central tendon (aponeurosis)
structures.role: Deep tendon within the proximal to mid belly onto which fibres insert. Strain around it is the 'red flag' injury with a longer rehabilitation [r2]

structures.name: Proximal tendons (direct and indirect heads)
structures.role: Origins from the AIIS and acetabular rim. AIIS avulsion in children, and tears in adults, are separate injury patterns [r3]

structures.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
structures.role: Monoarticular knee extensors. Vastus injuries had the shortest mean rehabilitation (4.4 days) in one MRI series [r2]

structures.name: Quadriceps tendon
structures.role: Joins the four heads and transmits force to the patella

structures.name: Femoral nerve and vessels
structures.role: Lie medially on the front of the thigh; relevant to a large haematoma or deep injury

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
A strain occurs when an active, contracting muscle is lengthened beyond the capacity of its weakest region. In the rectus femoris this is typically around the central tendon or the MTJ, where fibres insert onto the tendon [r2]. Torn fibres retract, capillaries bleed into the gap and a haematoma forms, then inflammation clears the debris, satellite cells regenerate fibres and a connective-tissue scar matures [r5]. Treatment principles for muscle injury have come largely from experimental studies or empirical practice, because few clinical studies exist [r5].

Site predicts recovery. In 25 MRI-confirmed quadriceps strains in Australian football, 15 involved the rectus femoris. Those about the central tendon (n = 7) had a mean rehabilitation interval of 26.9 days, against 9.2 days for peripheral injuries (n = 8), 4.4 days for vastus injuries (n = 6) and 5.7 days for MRI-negative injuries (n = 3) [r2]. In elite track and field, rectus femoris injuries extending into the tendon (British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) class c) and those managed surgically took longer to return to full training, and grade 3 injuries had higher repeat-injury rates [r13].

structures.name: Rectus femoris belly
structures.effect: Fibre disruption and haematoma, most often around the central tendon or MTJ [r2]

structures.name: Central tendon (aponeurosis)
structures.effect: Partial disruption in intratendinous (class c) injuries, which have longer return to training [r13,r2]

structures.name: Proximal tendons (AIIS and acetabular rim)
structures.effect: Enthesis, intratendinous or MTJ injury of either head; complete or retracted tears can need surgery [r3,r4]

structures.name: Vastus muscles
structures.effect: Less commonly strained, with a shorter rehabilitation interval [r2]

muscles.name: Rectus femoris and quadriceps
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition reduces knee extension and hip flexion strength early (clinical reasoning). Strength deficits, with loss of kicking power, are common until criteria are met.

muscles.name: Hip flexors (iliopsoas) and vasti
muscles.effect: Take over some hip flexion and knee extension during rehabilitation (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Hamstrings and gluteals
muscles.effect: A recent hamstring strain is itself a risk factor for quadriceps injury, which shows the link between the posterior and anterior thigh [r10].

muscles.name: Trunk and lumbopelvic muscles
muscles.effect: Control of pelvic tilt alters rectus femoris length in kicking and sprinting (mechanism reasoning).

cellular.description: Fibres rupture and their ends become necrotic. Torn capillaries form a haematoma [r5].
Neutrophils and then macrophages clear necrotic tissue [r5].
Satellite cells proliferate and form new myotubes. Fibroblasts lay down a connective-tissue scar and capillaries grow in [r5].
Regenerated fibres mature, and the scar remodels along the line of load as the athlete returns to loading [r5].

systems.effect: Nociception and pain inhibition reduce activation of the quadriceps and hip flexors. Protective guarding may persist after pain settles (clinical reasoning).
Intramuscular bleeding and inflammation produce swelling and pain. A large haematoma can lead to later complications such as myositis ossificans [r4].
Kicking and sprint mechanics depend on the whole chain. A previous hamstring injury is a risk factor, and the dominant kicking leg is at higher risk [r10].
Fear of re-injury at maximal kicking or sprinting is common and affects return. Psychological readiness is part of return-to-play decision-making in muscle injury consensus [r6].

grading.system: British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC), based on MRI [r14]

grades.prognosis: Shortest time to return; the 3 MRI-negative quadriceps injuries had a mean rehabilitation of 5.7 days in one series [r2]
Grade 1 rectus femoris injuries had a significantly shorter time to return to full training than grades 2 and 3 [r13]
Longer return and a higher repeat-injury rate than other grades in rectus femoris injuries [r13]

grades.description: Complete tear of the muscle or tendon (4c = complete tendon tear) [r14].
grades.prognosis: Four complete proximal free tendon injuries were reported in female sprinters; surgical management was associated with a longer return to training [r13]

grades.description: a = myofascial, b = musculotendinous junction, c = intratendinous [r14].
grades.prognosis: Class c (intratendinous) rectus femoris injuries had delayed return, and myofascial (a) injuries had fewer repeat injuries than b or c [r13]

timeframes.summary: Recovery depends on the site and extent of the injury. In 38 rectus femoris injuries in elite track and field athletes, the mean time to return to full training for rehabilitation-managed cases was 20.4 ± 14.8 days, with wide variation [r13]. These are elite-athlete figures and may not apply to recreational players. Re-injury after return causes longer absence [r15].

healing.description: Satellite-cell regeneration, scar formation and capillary ingrowth [r5]
Fibre maturation and scar realignment under progressive load [r5]

milestones.label: Normal walking, pain-free isometric contraction
milestones.note: Typical clinical range for a small injury

milestones.label: Start jogging
milestones.note: Once pain-free walking and strength criteria are met (clinical convention)

milestones.label: Peripheral rectus femoris injury: return to full training (mean)
milestones.note: Mean 9.2 days in 8 Australian football players [r2]

milestones.label: Rectus femoris injury, rehabilitation managed: return to full training (mean)
milestones.note: Mean 20.4 days in elite track and field athletes [r13]

milestones.label: Central tendon injury: return to full training (mean)
milestones.note: Mean 26.9 days in 7 Australian football players [r2]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, not time-based. Mean time to return to full training was 20.4 ± 14.8 days in rehabilitation-managed rectus femoris injuries in elite track and field athletes, and intratendinous and surgically managed injuries took significantly longer [r13]. Around the central tendon, the mean was 26.9 days in one small football series [r2].

symptoms: Sudden sharp pain in the front of the thigh during a kick or sprint acceleration, often with the athlete pulling up
Pain with hip flexion or knee extension [r4]
Pain with fast walking, stairs, running and kicking
Swelling in the anterior thigh, with bruising that may appear later
Loss of kicking power and a feeling of weakness
signs: Localised tenderness over the rectus femoris, usually in the proximal to mid thigh [r2]
Pain on resisted knee extension and resisted hip flexion
Pain on stretching the rectus femoris (knee flexion with the hip extended)
Swelling and, in severe injuries, a palpable gap [r4]
Antalgic gait with reduced knee flexion and a shortened stride

subjective: Mechanism: kicking (back-swing or ball contact), sprint acceleration or a stretch, and whether it was non-contact or a direct blow [r8]
Which leg: the dominant kicking leg is at higher risk [r10]
Previous quadriceps injury, recent hamstring strain, or ACL reconstruction with a patellar tendon graft [r10,r11]
Immediate loss of function, pain severity, swelling and bruising [r4]
Recent training, kicking and match load, including fixture congestion [r12]
Age (adolescent: apophyseal injury) and the demands of the sport and level [r3]
observation: Loss of the normal thigh contour or a visible defect
Ability to kick or accelerate at slow speed
palpation: Locate the point of maximal tenderness along the rectus femoris and compare it with the AIIS (proximal tendon), the proximal to mid belly (central tendon) and the lower muscle
Feel for a palpable gap or defect in the belly or at the tendon, which suggests a significant tendon injury [r4]
rangeOfMotion: Prone knee flexion with the hip extended (rectus femoris stretch, Ely test): pain or reduced range compared with the other side
Thomas test position for hip flexor and rectus femoris length
Active and passive hip extension and knee flexion
strength: Resisted knee extension at mid-range and near extension, and resisted hip flexion with the knee flexed and extended
Hand-held dynamometry of knee extension and hip flexion with side-to-side comparison
neuro: Femoral nerve screen: thigh sensation and knee extension power
Lumbar screen if anterior thigh symptoms have a neural pattern
functional: Hop tests and running at graded speeds

specialTests.name: Palpation of the rectus femoris and its tendons
specialTests.purpose: Localise the injury site and find a gap
specialTests.procedure: Palpate from the AIIS down the belly to the patella, with the muscle relaxed and then contracting, and compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness reproducing the pain, or a palpable defect. A gap with marked weakness suggests a complete tendon injury [r4]. No accuracy data were identified.

specialTests.name: Prone knee flexion test (Ely test)
specialTests.purpose: Provoke pain and measure rectus femoris length
specialTests.procedure: Prone, the examiner passively flexes the knee while the hip stays on the couch. Compare range and pain with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Pain in the anterior thigh or reduced knee flexion with the pelvis rising. No accuracy data were identified.

specialTests.name: Resisted knee extension and hip flexion
specialTests.purpose: Provocation and measure of strength deficit
specialTests.procedure: Seated or supine, ask for a maximal isometric contraction of knee extension (and hip flexion with the knee flexed) against resistance and compare sides.
specialTests.positive: Pain and weakness in the anterior thigh [r4]. No accuracy data were identified.

clinicalRules.name: Features that raise suspicion of a tendon injury
clinicalRules.description: A palpable gap, marked weakness, retraction or the mechanism of a violent kick or sprint suggests a complete tendon injury or avulsion, which can need operative treatment. MRI identifies retraction [r4].

clinicalRules.name: No validated rule for time to return
clinicalRules.description: No validated clinical prediction rule for time to return in quadriceps strain was identified. MRI findings (central tendon or intratendinous involvement, BAMIC grade) have been associated with longer return in small cohorts [r2,r13].

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain numerical rating scale (palpation, resisted tests and during sport tasks)
outcomeMeasures.use: Used to monitor progression and apply pain-based criteria (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Hand-held or isokinetic strength: limb symmetry for knee extension and hip flexion
outcomeMeasures.use: Track strength recovery before return (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: BAMIC grade from MRI
outcomeMeasures.use: Prognosis and communication. Grade and class c status were associated with return time in rectus femoris injuries [r13]

outcomeMeasures.name: Lower Extremity Functional Scale or a global rating of change
outcomeMeasures.use: Generic patient-reported function. No quadriceps-strain-specific validated questionnaire was identified

imaging.indication: Early confirmation of the injury, haematoma and retraction where MRI is unavailable
imaging.findings: Fibre disruption, haematoma and tendon discontinuity. Ultrasound and MRI help to determine the extent of the injury [r4]. Operator-dependent.

imaging.indication: Suspected tendon injury, elite athletes, an unclear diagnosis, or a recurrent injury. In the AFL series scans were done within 24–72 h and helped predict prognosis [r2]
imaging.findings: Site (central tendon, periphery, vastus or proximal tendon) and size. Central tendon injury is a 'red flag' with longer rehabilitation [r2]. BAMIC grade and class [r13]. Each head of the proximal tendon can be injured at the enthesis, within the tendon or at the MTJ, and MRI shows retraction that may need surgery [r3,r4].

imaging.indication: Adolescents with pain at the AIIS after a kick or sprint, or later if a hard mass or restricted flexion develops
imaging.findings: AIIS apophyseal avulsion in children [r3]; heterotopic ossification (myositis ossificans) is a recognised later complication [r4].

differentials.name: Quadriceps contusion and myositis ossificans
differentials.distinguishing: Direct blow, with tenderness and swelling at the impact site and no kicking or sprint mechanism. Loss of knee flexion and a hard mass weeks later suggest myositis ossificans.

differentials.name: Pelvic apophyseal avulsion (AIIS)
differentials.distinguishing: Adolescent with an open apophysis and pain at the AIIS after a kick or sprint; a fragment on radiograph.

differentials.name: Iliopsoas-related groin pain
differentials.distinguishing: Deeper anterior hip or groin pain with resisted hip flexion and a painful stretch in hip extension, without focal tenderness along the rectus femoris belly.

differentials.name: Rectus femoris proximal tendinopathy or tear
differentials.distinguishing: Pain nearer the AIIS and the inguinal region, often with a gradual onset or a long kicking history; MRI shows the tendon pattern [r3].

differentials.name: Distal quadriceps tendon rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Pain at the superior pole of the patella, a gap above the patella and inability to extend the knee against gravity.

differentials.name: Femoral neck stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Groin or anterior thigh pain with weight-bearing and night pain, hop-test pain and a rise in running volume; MRI shows bone oedema.

differentials.name: Lumbar radiculopathy (femoral nerve roots)
differentials.distinguishing: Back pain, anterior thigh symptoms with a neural pattern, and reduced reflexes or dermatomal sensation, without focal tenderness.

redFlags: A palpable gap, marked weakness of knee extension or hip flexion, or retraction after a violent kick or sprint: suspect a complete tendon injury or avulsion. Arrange MRI and orthopaedic review, as these can need surgery [r4].
Adolescent with AIIS pain after kicking or sprinting: radiograph to look for an apophyseal avulsion [r3].
Rapidly increasing tense thigh swelling with severe pain out of proportion, especially on anticoagulants: suspect compartment syndrome or a large haematoma and refer urgently.
A hard, growing mass or progressive loss of knee flexion weeks after injury: suspect myositis ossificans or, rarely, a tumour masquerading as a haematoma. Arrange imaging [r4].
Calf swelling, pain or breathlessness after injury or immobilisation: suspect DVT or pulmonary embolism and arrange same-day medical review.
Constant or night pain unrelated to activity, weight loss, fever or a history of cancer: suspect bone or soft-tissue pathology and arrange urgent medical review.

management.principles: Most quadriceps strains are managed without surgery, through early, graded loading adapted to the site and extent of the injury [r5,r4]. No randomised trials of treatment for quadriceps strain were identified, so rehabilitation draws on muscle-injury principles [r5] and on hamstring-injury consensus, which advises individualised rehabilitation based on the athlete, sporting demands, the muscles involved and injury severity, and avoiding high strain loads and rates in the early stage [r6]. Use MRI when a tendon injury is suspected, in elite athletes, or when the picture is unclear, because central tendon and intratendinous injuries need longer [r2,r13]. Complete tendon injuries and avulsions can need operative treatment [r4]. Make return-to-play decisions together with the athlete, medical staff and coach, and expect higher re-injury cost: re-injuries led to longer absences than index injuries [r15].

medical.name: Acute-phase rest, ice and compression
medical.description: A short phase of relative rest, ice and compression is suggested for the acute phase, together with a designed return-to-play protocol [r4]. Do not immobilise for long [r5].

medical.name: Analgesia and short-term NSAIDs
medical.description: Simple analgesia for the first days. NSAIDs may relieve early pain, but their effect on muscle healing is uncertain, so keep courses short. Muscle-healing evidence has largely come from experimental studies [r5].

medical.name: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection
medical.description: No quadriceps trial was identified. In a double-blind RCT of 80 athletes with acute hamstring injuries, PRP did not accelerate return to play, and at 1 year there was no benefit for re-injury (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.38–2.13) [r16]. Do not extrapolate a benefit to the quadriceps.

medical.name: Surgical repair of complete or retracted tendon injuries
medical.description: Complete tendon injuries and avulsions can need operative treatment, and MRI can identify retraction [r4]. Surgically managed rectus femoris injuries had a longer time to return to full training in elite track and field [r13]. Surgery is not used for intramuscular strains.

physio.name: Staged, criteria-based loading programme
physio.description: Progress from isometric to isotonic to heavy and long-length loading, then running, acceleration and kicking, using pain and strength criteria rather than time. There are no quadriceps-specific trials. The approach follows muscle-injury principles and hamstring consensus, which supports capacity-based progression and criteria for running and return to sport [r5,r6].

physio.name: Graded kicking and sprint exposure
physio.description: Rectus femoris injuries occur in repetitive kicking and sprinting [r1]. Build up kicking distance and sprint speed in steps, monitoring pain and quality. The hamstring consensus supports pain-free sprinting before return [r6].

physio.name: Long-length (lengthened-state) rectus femoris loading
physio.description: Include loading of the rectus femoris with the hip extended and the knee flexed (for example rear-foot-elevated split squats or reverse Nordic lowering) in later stages, since this is the length at which the muscle is injured in kicking (mechanism reasoning).

physio.name: Hip, pelvis and trunk control and kinetic-chain work
physio.description: Gluteal, hamstring and trunk strengthening and control of pelvic tilt in kicking and sprinting. A recent hamstring strain is a risk factor for quadriceps injury [r10].

physio.name: Aggressive early stretching of the quadriceps
physio.description: Stretching the rectus femoris into pain in the first days can aggravate the injury. Use graded loading instead (clinical reasoning).

physio.name: Prolonged rest or immobilisation
physio.description: A brief period of relative rest is enough. Prolonged immobilisation is not advised, because the understanding of muscle healing supports early graded mobilisation [r5].

physio.name: Passive modalities alone (massage, therapeutic ultrasound, electrotherapy)
physio.description: No quadriceps-specific evidence was identified. Passive treatment does not rebuild strength or kicking tolerance. Use it only as an adjunct.

education: A quadriceps strain is a tear in the muscle at the front of the thigh. Most heal well with a planned, progressive program.
How long it takes depends on where the tear is. Tears near the central tendon take longer, and an MRI can help to explain this.
Some discomfort during exercise is acceptable if it settles quickly, but sharp pain means the load was too high. Avoid forced stretching in the first days.
Return to kicking and sprinting is decided by tests, not by the date. Returning too early is a common cause of re-injury.
If you have a gap, a hard lump, or the swelling is increasing quickly, tell your clinician promptly.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and built around four themes: restore tolerance to load, rebuild strength through the range, load the rectus femoris at length and at speed, then return to kicking and sprinting. No quadriceps-specific rehabilitation trials were identified, so the stages follow muscle-injury principles and hamstring-injury consensus, which supports individualised, capacity- and symptom-based progression, avoiding high strain loads and rates early, and pain-free sprinting before return [r5,r6]. Timeframes are typical for a rectus femoris injury of the muscle belly (compare a mean of 20.4 days to return to full training in elite track and field [r13]); expect slower progress for central tendon, intratendinous or proximal tendon injuries [r2,r13]. Dosages are typical clinical ranges and not trial-derived. As a working rule, mild pain (3/10 or less) during exercise is acceptable if it settles within 24 hours (clinical convention).

stages.name: Protect & early loading
goals: Pain-free submaximal isometric knee extension and hip flexion
precautions: No forced stretching, kicking or sprinting
Screen for a gap, retraction or marked weakness and arrange MRI if present [r4]
Use crutches only if the athlete cannot walk without a limp

exercises.name: Quadriceps set and isometric knee extension at several angles
exercises.dosage: 5 × 5 holds of 5–10 s at 30–70% effort, 2–3 times daily
exercises.cues: Build tension slowly and stay within tolerable discomfort

exercises.name: Isometric hip flexion (supine or seated)
exercises.cues: Press the thigh gently into the hand or band

exercises.name: Double-leg glute bridge
exercises.cues: Push through the heels and keep the pelvis level

progressionCriteria: Pain at or below 3/10 on submaximal isometric knee extension and hip flexion

stages.name: Strength through range
goals: Restore knee extension and hip flexion strength through range
precautions: Increase load only if symptoms settle within 24 hours
No maximal sprinting or kicking yet
Introduce range gradually; avoid loading at long length too soon

exercises.name: Squat to box (progressing depth and load)
exercises.cues: Knees over toes, weight through the whole foot

exercises.name: Split squat
exercises.cues: Torso upright; front knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Step-ups
exercises.cues: Drive through the heel and keep the pelvis level

exercises.name: Seated knee extension (isotonic)
exercises.cues: Work in the pain-free range first

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.cues: Hinge at the hips with a long spine

exercises.name: Progressive straight-line jogging
exercises.dosage: Intervals at 50–70% of maximal speed, every other day
exercises.cues: Relaxed and tall; stop if pain increases

progressionCriteria: Pain-free resisted knee extension and hip flexion
Knee extension strength at least 80% of the other side (clinical convention)
Pain-free jogging at 70% of maximal speed

stages.name: Long-length loading, power & running
goals: Load the rectus femoris with the hip extended and the knee flexed
precautions: Introduce long-length and plyometric loading at low volume (expect soreness for 24–48 hours)
Progress sprint speed in steps of about 10%
Stop if pain at the anterior thigh increases

exercises.name: Rear-foot-elevated split squat
exercises.cues: Let the back hip extend as the front knee bends; keep the trunk tall

exercises.name: Reverse Nordic lowering
exercises.cues: Kneel, lean back slowly through the thighs, keep the hips extended

exercises.name: Jump squat and drop landing
exercises.cues: Soft landing with hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Single-leg hop progressions
exercises.cues: Quiet landing; stick it for 2 s

exercises.name: Acceleration runs and drills (A-skips, high knees)
exercises.dosage: 3–4 sets of 20 m, 2–3 times a week, building to 85–95% of maximal speed
exercises.cues: Drive the knee and keep the pelvis level

progressionCriteria: Knee extension and hip flexion strength at least 90% of the other side
Pain-free sprinting at 90–95% of maximal speed
No pain on resisted tests or on rectus femoris stretch (Ely test) compared with the other side

stages.name: Kicking & return to sport
goals: Full sport-specific training including maximal sprints and change of direction
precautions: Build kicking distance and power in steps and stop if pain returns
Plan the first matches with limited minutes and avoid fixture congestion [r12]
Monitor load as match exposure rises

exercises.name: Graded kicking: short passes to full-power long kicks
exercises.dosage: Start at 10–20 kicks and build in steps, 2–3 sessions a week
exercises.cues: Quality contact; stop if pain returns

exercises.name: Repeated maximal sprints and sport-specific drills
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sessions a week within team training
exercises.cues: Include fatigued sprinting and kicking where relevant

exercises.name: Back-swing control and long-length strength
exercises.dosage: 2–3 × 6–8 reverse Nordic or rear-foot-elevated split squats, 1–2 times a week

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance (squat, split squat, hip thrust)

progressionCriteria: Completion of full team training without symptoms
Athlete confidence at full-power kicking and maximal sprinting

criteria: No quadriceps-specific return-to-play criteria were identified in the sources reviewed. The criteria below follow hamstring-injury consensus, which supports individualised, capacity-based criteria and pain-free sprinting [r6], and clinical convention
No pain on palpation of the rectus femoris and its tendons (clinical convention)
No pain and no side-to-side deficit on resisted knee extension and hip flexion, and rectus femoris length (Ely test) similar to the other side (clinical convention)
Knee extension and hip flexion strength at least 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Pain-free maximal sprinting [r6] and full-power kicking
Completion of sport-specific training, psychological readiness and a shared decision with the athlete and staff [r6]
tests: Palpation and resisted knee extension and hip flexion
Ely test and Thomas test compared with the other side
Hand-held or isokinetic dynamometry of knee extension and hip flexion
Maximal sprint with timing gates or GPS
Graded kicking test at full power

prognosis: Most athletes return to sport, but re-injury is a problem. In male professional footballers 16% of muscle injuries were re-injuries and caused longer absences than index injuries [r7], and re-injuries led to longer absence for quadriceps muscle injuries and five other diagnoses [r15]. Site and grade predict recovery: central tendon and intratendinous injuries took longer [r2,r13], and grade 3 rectus femoris injuries had higher repeat-injury rates [r13]. A previous quadriceps injury is itself the strongest risk factor for a future one [r10]. Long-term outcome data were not identified in the sources reviewed.
prevention: No quadriceps-specific prevention trials were identified. The measures below come from risk-factor evidence and clinical reasoning.
Pay attention to the highest-risk athletes: those with a previous quadriceps injury, a recent hamstring strain or a patellar tendon ACL graft, and kicking-dominant players [r10,r11].
Manage load around the preseason and during fixture congestion, when muscle injury rates were higher [r10,r12].
Keep a strength programme for the quadriceps, hips and hamstrings, and include kicking and sprint exposure in training (clinical reasoning) [r1].
Complete criteria-based rehabilitation before return, since re-injury leads to longer absence [r15].
clinicalPearls: Where the tear is matters. Rectus femoris injury about the central tendon took a mean of 26.9 days against 9.2 days at the periphery in a small AFL series, so palpate the site and consider MRI [r2].
The kicking leg is the injured leg more often. Ask about previous quadriceps and hamstring injuries, because both are risk factors [r10].
A palpable gap, marked weakness or retraction after a violent kick means tendon injury until proved otherwise. MRI identifies retraction that may need surgery [r4].
In adolescents, anterior hip pain after a kick is an AIIS avulsion until a radiograph says otherwise [r3].
Do not assume one rectus femoris injury equals another. Intratendinous (c) injuries and grade 3 injuries had longer return and more repeat injuries in elite track and field athletes [r13].
After ACL reconstruction with a patellar tendon graft, expect more quadriceps injuries on return to play (RR 3.5 against the 2 years before the ACL injury) [r11].

animation.title: How a rectus femoris (quadriceps) strain happens

forces.label: Rectus femoris stretched over hip and knee
Explosive hip flexion and knee extension

captions.text: A footballer runs on to the ball to take a full-power kick with the right foot.
In the back-swing the hip extends and the knee flexes, so the rectus femoris is stretched over both joints.
The muscle then contracts forcefully to drive the hip and knee through ball contact.
Load exceeds capacity: a sudden sharp pain in the front of the thigh.
The athlete pulls up and grabs the anterior thigh.
Zooming into the front of the right thigh, viewed from the front.

actions.text: Rectus femoris: crosses hip and knee
Strain near the central tendon and MTJ
Proximal tendon at the AIIS: avulsion in adolescents

captions.text: The rectus femoris runs from the pelvis to the patella, crossing both the hip and the knee.
In a kick, the muscle is stretched over both joints and then contracts hard.
Fibres tear next to the central tendon and musculotendinous junction, the most common site.
Torn capillaries bleed into the muscle, forming a haematoma.
If the tear involves the central tendon, return to training takes longer.
Pain sits in the proximal to mid thigh and is provoked by hip flexion and knee extension.
Proximal tendon injuries, and AIIS avulsion in teenagers, are separate patterns.
Healthy muscle: myofibres made of aligned sarcomeres.
Actin and myosin cross-bridges generate force as the fibre contracts.
The active fibre is forcibly lengthened beyond its capacity.
Sarcomeres overstretch and rupture, and the fibres retract from the tear.
Torn capillaries bleed and a haematoma fills the gap.
Neutrophils and macrophages clear necrotic fibre ends.
Satellite cells activate and proliferate beneath the basal lamina.
New myotubes form and fuse with surviving fibres.
A connective-tissue scar matures. Graded loading helps it align and strengthen.
